GARTH, father of Jane, three weeks The birth 17 The birth The birth of your child is a major event in your life. It is the end of the waiting after nine months and the start of a new life, the formal beginning of a relationship, the first page of a lifelong story. Many men now choose to be present at the births of their children. Your role But what is your role during birth, and who are you there for—yourself, your partner, or your newborn child? The answer should be "all three." You are witnessing part of your own history. You are supporting the person closest to you as she goes through what can be a difficult physical and emotional experience to give birth to the child you have both created and nurtured. And you are welcoming a new member of your family. For many men it is a deeply moving, almost miraculous event, but it can also be distressing if you see your partner in pain, or if you don't understand what is happening if medical complications set in. Playing your part In order to play a full role, make sure you understand the mechanics of birth. You will be of little use to your partner if you have to keep asking her or the doctor or midwife what is happening. You should also take time to talk through with your partner how she wants to handle the birth and pain relief. She may have written down a birth plan (see below). When she's in the middle of the emotions of labor, she will rely on you to make her wishes plain to her healthcare providers. And, in advance of the event, consider realistically how you are going to handle your own emotions and fears about witnessing the birth of your child. The birth plan Doctors and midwives often advise couples to write down a birth plan before their baby is due to be born. Circumstances may intervene, but it enables you to approach labor with a clear view of how you both would like it to proceed. Since it is your partner who will go through the Expert tips There are several good reasons for being at the birth of your child: • because it is a life-changing experience to see your child born • to support your partner • to help her communicate with healthcare providers | • to welcome your child. physical experience of labor, hers must be the guiding voice. Try to stay open-minded, however. This is only a rough guide, and once labor begins, your partner may change her mind about some of the plans. A written birth plan should cover the following areas: • who will attend the birth • your partner's views on induction • what pain relief she wants • what position she would like to be in for labor 18 Being a dad WRITING A BIRTH PLAN Writing a birth plan with your partner helps you both to be clear on what her wishes are once labor starts. Checklist The following are things you'll need to have ready to take to the hospital: plenty of change (remember, you can't use a cell phone in the hospital, so you will have to use the pay phone); a list of telephone numbers of key relatives and friends; some drinks and snacks, since it may be a long time before you have a chance to go to the hospital cafeteria; a camera for the first shot of your newborn child. Your partner's bag should include: nightgowns and a bathrobe; two maternity bras; breast pads; sanitary pads; several pairs of underpants (either cotton or disposable); clothes to go home in; toiletries (toothbrush and toothpaste, washcloth, towel, hairbrush, shampoo, lotion, makeup). For your baby you will need: diapers and baby wipes; onesies or sleepers; a sweater or coat and a hat to go home in; a blanket; a car seat. • what position she would like to be in for birth • what medical procedures she will consent to during birth • what she would like tire medical staff to do with the baby as soon as it arrives (hand it straight to you, for example) • her attitude to breastfeeding • thoughts on possible birth complications, such as emergency cesareans or intervention to speed up labor. The birth 19 What will happen Whether you and your partner have decided on a home birth or a hospital delivery, you will be joined at the birth by at least one healthcare provider. If it is a home birth, you may well find yourself playing a practical role as assistant midwife. In the hospital, in addition to the nursing staff, there will usually be doctors present. They will all be eager for you to participate as fully as possible in the birth. Being a supporter We naturally defer to doctors, so it may be tempting to play along and adopt a background role by leaving your partner in "expert hands." But if you want it, there is a vital role for you as your partner's supporter and advocate. She will be able to see you, the father of the child soon to be born, amid potentially unfamiliar medical faces. She may want to discuss with you the professional advice she is getting from her healthcare providers and compare it with the birth plan that you have worked out together beforehand. There may be occasions when what seems to the medical staff to be the best way forward doesn't quite match up with what \ your partner feels her body ( is telling her. Listen to what your partner is saying. Support her in her choices and politely but firmly pass on any views or concerns she wants to communicate to the hospital staff. The experience of seeing the one you love in pain can be disconcerting, but pain, you must remember, is a natural part of childbirth. Your protective instinct may make you want to force the medical staff to administer pain relief, but stop for a moment and weigh this against what your partner has decided in her birth plan. Resist the urge to try to take over. Recognize the uniqueness of the situation and make sure you keep a level head. Three stages of labor The first stage: the cervix opens up (dilates) to allow the baby's head to pass through. Contractions thin, soften, and stretch the cervix. Dilation is measured in centimeters, up to a maximum of around 10. This can be a long process, especially with a first labor. The second stage: this is shorter, usually no more than two hours. Your partner will feel a reflex to push down during contractions. Gradually the baby's head will appear, leading to delivery. The third stage: this lasts from delivery until the uterus contracts again to expel the placenta— usually after 15 minutes or so. A SUPPORTING ROLE Rubbing your partner's back will help ease the pain as she copes with contractions. 20 Being a dad Ways to help during labor Labor can be a very lengthy process, and while your partner is in the midst of it, there will be many ways in which you can help and encourage her: • rubbing her back to ease the pain caused by the contractions • supporting her weight as she adopts some of the pain-relieving positions learned in prenatal classes • wiping her forehead • encouraging her and even joining her in breathing exercises • providing a steady supply of drinks and, if she wants it, energy¬ giving food • putting on soothing music • distracting her from tine pain by reading, talking, or playing games • feeling and timing her contractions • filling in insurance forms. Safety valve There may be times during labor when your partner's pain is such that she just has to let off steam and shout at someone. She may do it with the medical staff. They have plenty of experience with women in labor and will know how to handle this. Be prepared, too, for her to shout at you. Respond calmly with soothing words of praise and encouragement. She is only taking it out on you because she loves you and knows that she can. After the birth Once your baby has been delivered, a nurse or the midwife will clean him or her up. The baby will be returned to you after a couple of minutes. Usually, while your partner receives further medical attention- removal of the placenta, for example—you will be given your child to hold. It is a moment when it is impossible not to be emotional. Don’t feel shy about letting your feelings out. The medical staff will have seen fathers cry many times before. Your bonding with your child has begun. The medical staff will quickly start to peel away and give you time to be alone with your partner and your child. Don't rush this most precious moment. Your partner may want to The birth 21 talk over the labor with you, or about what you saw and what she experienced. She may also simply want you to join her in gazing in adoration at the tiny boy or girl in front of you. An odd hiatus If the labor has been a complicated one, or if your partner has had a cesarean, she may have to stay in the hospital to recover. You will be tired and feel tempted to go home and sleep. Don't feel bad about this. Your energy will be needed in abundance soon enough. If you have other children, they will need your special love and attention during a time that may be challenging for them. Questions & Answers Should I watch as the baby emerges from my partner's body? This is something you can discuss with your partner before the birth, but once you are both caught up in the labor, your feelings may change. For some men, it is part of the most extraordinary thing they will ever witness, and watching helps in the bonding process with their child. For others, the sight during a natural birth of what had previously been an intimate part of their partner's body in such a raw state may be disturbing. You will have a strong instinct which way to go when you are in the labor room. My wife wants to watch the baby coming out. How can I help? You can position and hold a mirror that will enable her to watch as she pushes. Whatever you do, don't get in the way of the hospital staff and don't offer a running commentary unless asked. Your partner will be preoccupied with what her body is going through and she doesn't need any distractions. What should I do when the baby first comes out? The medical staff usually places the baby, still attached by its umbilical cord, on your partner's body so she can see and hold the new arrival. Some couples find it soothing for the man at this stage to put his arms around both mother and child. It keeps them warm and signals that the three of you are a unit. Can I cut the umbilical cord? If the birth has been straightforward, there will be no medical objection to your doing this. Modern practice is to do it within the first 10 to 15 minutes after birth. It is another way of feeling part of the process, but it may not be for the squeamish. 22 Being a dad How can I bond with my newborn? By the end of the first week, given sufficient exposure to you, your baby will recognize you and your smell, and you will already begin to get a sense of the personality that is unfolding before you. By six weeks there will be smiles; by 12 weeks, chuckles. The bonding process is all about love, acceptance, and celebration. For your partner, especially if she is breastfeeding, there is a natural hormonal bonding impetus. The baby needs feeding and she is the one who can do it. For you, die routes to bonding are different, but no less instinctive. Touch and sound Hold your baby. If your partner is breastfeeding she will probably take on die majority of the childcare in the first few weeks, but retreating into housekeeping and domestic chores isn't the sum total of your role. Take every chance you can to pick up and cuddle your child. Dads who care for babies physically start to get fascinated and very in tune with them. This is called engrossment. Time If at first your baby doesn't settle easily with you and wants your partner, take it in stride. You will get the hang of it. Because you cannot give the immediate comfort of breast milk, it may take you a Me time to learn how to meet your child's needs. Be confident and work your way through different ways of calming until you discover the right ones. HOLDING AND CUDDLING Pick up your baby and cuddle her every time you get a chance, and the bonding process will simply happen almost without your being aware of it. FUNNY FACES Make time to do nothing but watch your baby. Get to know her range of little movements and savor the amazing array of funny faces she makes, especially when she's asleep. Euphoria Amid the chaos of the first weeks with a small baby, try to maintain a sense of the sheer wonder of being a father, of having created new life, and of nurturing that life. Make time to watch your baby while she sleeps, see her eyes scrunching up, twitching in the middle of dreams, her little fists clenching and unclenching, her arms reaching out and stretching before she falls back into a deep sleep. These magical moments, which you can savor, will all help strengthen the bonds forming between you. PRACTICAL BONDING Although you can't breastfeed your new baby, there are other practical things you can do that will help you bond with her—diaper¬ changing being a fine example! " I went into parenthood with my eyes wide open but it has exceeded my expectations so much that it is all the harder to juggle my work and my home life." PHILIP, father of Rowan, three months What is a dad's role? 25 What is a dad's role? The i ole of fathers has come under more sustained scrutiny in recent times than ever before. This is partly because of the evolution in women's roles in society in the developed world. As women increasingly seek career opportunities outside the home, should that leave dad holding the baby? What's right for you As a response to such questions, we are now bombarded with media images of fathers—be they the lone dads of Hollywood movies, the weekend dads created by the ever- increasing demands of the workplace, or the dads trying and often failing to juggle all their responsibilities in the modern two-income family. Which of these composites fits your life? Probably none. Each of us has to cope with our circumstances as best we can and attempt, in consultation with our partner, to forge our own model of fatherhood. There are no right or wrong answers—just what suits you, your partner, and your child. And there should be no guilt. This is the most destructive of emotions. Co-parenting At one time, the idea of fathering was seen principally in its biological context—literally begetting a child. Mothering, by contrast, included the notion of caring and nurturing. In today's world, such distinctions are obsolete. Parenting sums up the ambition for dads to be intimately involved alongside mothers in their children's development, but beyond the fine words, how exactly do you put that into practice? Paternal role models There are many different role models for dads. None is right or wrong, but together they cover the whole spectrum from the mythical "superdad" who can simultaneously change a diaper, warm up a bottle, and hold a conference call on his cell phone with colleagues about a global merger, to the equally mythical absentee father who would scarcely recognize his child in a school photograph. Following any preordained pattern for being a dad is a recipe for disaster. You must be yourself first and foremost. What matters most is not the quantity of time you spend with your children, but how you act when you spend time together. If your children feel that you connect with them, if you can show them warmth, kindness, and love, if you can think yourself out of your other everyday concerns and into their mindset, then you will be a good dad, and your What is a dad's role? 27 relationship will flourish. With other adults, you forge a relationship by spending time together and getting to know them. This is how it is with your baby. Never too early Some experts believe you should start reading to babies while they are still in the womb, but it will be in the second half of the first year that your child can become an active participant in the reading process—if only by chewing the corners of the books you are reading to her! The rhythm and sound of the words rather than their meanings will be the first things to make an impact, followed by the colors, patterns, and shapes in the illustrations. Tone of voice Tone and inflection are key components when you read aloud to your child. Don't imagine you are speaking to an adult audience from a podium or presenting the news on television. If you need prompting as to what catches a child's attention, tune in to a children's TV program and listen to the presenters' style of delivery. Make your voice sing-song, not monotonous; add exaggerated emphasis; and repeat yourself to convey the detail. If what you are reading is funny, laugh out loud and then watch your child imitate you. READING TOGETHER Looking at books together and reading to your child will help her develop a love of books that she will retain throughout her life. she will make sense of the world, overcome her fears, and learn to relate to others. • Face to face Design your games around staying in face-to-face contact. Our faces are the most expressive part of us and the most obvious channel for communicating the love and information that will help your baby grow. • Rough-and-tumble Make as much noise as you like, and incorporate suitable elements of rough-and-tumble into your play. Dads can have a special role in nurturing the physical aspect of their children's development. Landmarks Even the most mundane activity can be turned into a treat for your child if you have the right attitude. If it has to be done, you have the choice of making it a chore or making it an adventure. A car ride, for example, can be an occasion for joyous singing and giggles, or you can make a trip to the supermarket a fun time—and shoulder your part of domestic life at the same time. Small children need little encouragement to delight in the bright colors and lights of these consumer temples. A program of child-centered, educational trips and activities is not necessary. With the right attitude TIME OUT When you take your baby out for a walk, interact with her by talking about what you can see—the leaves on the trees and the clouds in the sky, for example. on your part and with your commitment of time, the weekend chores can be the ultimate learning opportunity. Even if you don't feel up to it, be positive and creative. Don't retreat behind the newspaper at breakfast time, but play airplanes with a spoonful of cereal. Don't sit glued to the news on television or stay in bed until noon on Saturday morning. Your child's childhood will pass quickly enough, so make sure you get involved and are a part of it. Sleep time Once your baby has passed the eight-week stage, she should be ready to settle into a sleeping pattern. By a happy coincidence, the most Expert tip 48 Being a dad SHARED CARE Caring for your child is a responsibility you can share with your partner—and like all the other activities you do with your child, it can be bonding, rewarding, and fun. natural time for her to go to sleep— around 7 o'clock in the evening—is also the time that many working dads arrive home. What better way to change gear from breadwinner to nurturing father than to get involved in the going-to-bed ritual and make it your special time. Older siblings As your children get older, the basic patterns of family life will be for you and your partner to share yourselves, both as a couple and as individuals, equally between your children in terms of love, affection, time, outings, and so on. At this early stage, however, your partner may still be breastfeeding, and if you have older children they may feel that their mother’s attention is rather lop-sided in favor of the new arrival. In such a situation, dads can be a great corrective. An older sibling's envying a new brother or sister is perfectly natural. Most big brothers and sisters go through a stage where they want to be a baby again—so they can replace the infant sibling on their mother's lap or even at her breast. Be prepared for some regressive behavior. It isn’t a big deal. Constant requests to "be a good big Bedtime stories work well for dads who are just home from work, but you can, of course, read together at any time. Have books lying around so they are always on hand to fill a spare five minutes or to assist you in distracting or calming an unhappy child. Make books seem normal by having them available, not extraordinary by keeping them high on a shelf out of your child's reach. For very young children, small, sturdy books are best because they let you lay them flat while you read, and your child can help turn the chunky pages. Vinyl books are good for bathtime. Rhymes have a strong appeal to the ears, and books that include activities contribute to making storytime fun. brother/sister" or "set a good example" are not the best policy and can often cause resentment. As tine parent with more freedom and flexibility in these early stages, you can take time to indulge older siblings a little by way of compensation, to praise their grown¬ up attributes, to point out all they can do that the baby can’t, and to reassure them that family life as they have come to know it will soon resume. The arrival of a new baby will inevitably have disturbed your usual routine, lrips and outings may have fallen by the wayside. The first year 49 ROUTINE REQUIREMENTS Developing a bedtime routine and sticking to it will greatly help your child learn to fall asleep easily. Bedtime Here are a few practical tips to help make bedtime easier. • Build up gradually to bedtime with a bath, reading a story, lots of hugs, kisses, and cuddles, then dimming the lights. • Perhaps combine the extended bedtime ritual with a final drink of water from a cup (once your baby is no longer being exclusively breastfed). Don’t worry about establishing a precedent. She will grow out of bedtime drinks naturally later on. • Devote yourself completely to what you're doing (so much so that you could easily fall asleep, too). If your baby senses that you are anxious for her to nod off so that you can get on with other things, she will fight sleep even harder because she doesn't want you to go away. • Keep to your routine and make changes or adjustments gradually. The security that comes from an endlessly repeating process will, in time, aid sleep. Make time to take your older children out, to have fun with them, to give them your full attention, and to listen to their views. Talk positively with them about their new brother or sister and how much they will add to family life once they have grown a little. " I have a great relationship with my daughter, and when my son was born, I wondered how different it would be. I've quickly discovered they both need me just the same." LEE, father of Esther, three years, and Jack, six months Boys and girls 51 Boys and girls Are men more interested in being fathers to sons, and is it the natural role of dads to focus on their sons and moms on their daughters? One organization that runs parenthood seminars reports that in most classes the ratio of men to women is 1 to 4. However, when the topic is raising boys, it is more like 1 to 1. A changing picture In short, the answer to the questions above is "yes" on both counts. We identify with our own sex more easily. Dads know what it's like to grow up as a boy. Part of that is how to develop masculinity, and dads clearly feel, with some justification, that they have much to contribute here, although in their absence, single moms often manage very well. Yet while it may be traditional for dads to concentrate their parenting on boys and moms on girls, that picture is inevitably changing in an age when men's and women's roles in society at large are becoming increasingly interchangeable. Love is all you need It is possible in our postfeminist age to get too tied up with gender. For children, the gender of the parents caring for them is much less important than if they can show warmth and kindness. Parents, meanwhile, love their children for who they are rather than what they are. The key to success as a parent is to be yourself, with your unique cocktail of what are still labeled masculine and feminine qualities. Your children know nothing about labels. They will learn from what you are, not from your gender. Dads are for everyone This is especially true with babies. Babies are babies, not boy babies or girl babies. It doesn't concern them, and we shouldn't worry about it too much, either By toddlerhood, however, boys tend to move around more and occupy more space. In general, they like the more vigorous kind of play that dads can offer. Rough-and-tumble with dad is a special treat and discharges pent-up energy and aggression that accompanies testosterone spurts in these years. Gender differences The differences between boys and girls: • are few compared to their similarities • are only tendencies • don't apply to every individual, or your children • don't have to be accepted by you. Fathering and mothering are not always the same. They are two complementary but ultimately different kinds of input. Dads, for example, are often better at robust play, while moms excel at calming children down. The two sets of skills work together, so having a mother and father present and active in their lives gives children the best chance of growing into happy, well- balanced adults—although they can, of course, reach the same point with solo parents or same sex parents. AVOIDING STEREOTYPES Cooking with your son, no matter what the outcome, can be fun and provide some calm time for talking. Dads and boys In a traditional two-parent family, the principal source of information about masculinity is from the dad. The first thing you need to do is to decide what you feel masculinity is all about so you won't confuse your sons—or, indeed, your daughters. Here are some questions you might like to consider. • How far is masculinity bound up with traditionally "male" interests such as sports, cars, or just "hanging out with the guys"? • How do you reconcile popular images of men being tough with the nurturing role you take on in your home? • How do you show love and affection and still be masculine? • Does your attitude to this differ in private and in public? • Do you care if people—other men in particular—regard you as unmasculine? • How do you feel men should behave toward women? Dads and girls There is, of course, no reason why dads cannot encourage their daughters to be great soccer players or to have high career ambitions. Both parents should avoid male and female stereotypes at this early stage Boys and girls 53 and allow their children room to be their own people. It is the best way of preparing them for the world where equal opportunities are now each individual's right. Gender equality Saying boys are different can easily develop into saying they are not as good as girls. With girls increasingly turning the tables on boys in some SOCCER SKILLS areas of educational achievement, it seems strange to us that previous generations of parents thought that girls were fundamentally different from boys and, for example, could never have careers in industry, science, or business. There is a move now to reestablish equal opportunities for boys and girls, and dads have a special role to play in achieving that goal. Why dads matter Boys growing up with an absentee father are statistically more likely to: • get physically injured • be violent • get into trouble • do poorly at school • be a member of a teenage gang in adolescence. Girls growing up with an absentee father are statistically more likely to: • have low self-esteem • have sex before they're ready • drop out of school. Don't make the assumption that your daughter won't enjoy sports as much as your son—given the opportunity, she will probably be just as enthusiastic. 54 Being a dad How can I be a positive role model? Being a positive role model boils down to setting a good example for your children— both sons and daughters—for life. By offering and demonstrating love, warmth, and kindness, and by taking an active role in their lives, you can show them that men make great dads, and that great dads are great parents. mm Boys and girls 55 HEALTHY OFFERINGS Set a good example for your children by cooking healthy meals for your family. Be a good parent Make fatherhood as natural as it is manly. Express feelings as well as indulging in vigorous activities; earn money and help out at home; teach baseball skills but know how to bake cookies. Be the best advertisement for the joys, achievements, and satisfaction of fatherhood that you can be. Do as I do What they see you do, your children will copy. Just because you have been out at work all day, you are not exempt from following house rules when you are at home. So eating unhealthily, for example, especially when your partner has spent all week coaxing your children off potato chips and onto apples, is not setting a good example. You might also consider that a good diet increases the odds that you will be around later on. Most of the causes of early death in men in the developed world—cancer, heart disease, strokes— are affected by what you eat. Try new hobbies Have a range of interests and hobbies, and be prepared to increase them in search of things you can do with your children. Swimming or cycling, for example, are sports you can do side by side. Encourage your children to widen their horizons by taking the plunge with them in a spirit of adventure. Happy home Be relaxed with your partner in front of your children. Show them how strong your love is for their mother and thus give them reassurance about the basic security of their home life and a positive model of co-parenting for the future. 11 Once Tim started running around, I found it harder to leave him and go out to work. As my relationship with him grows and deepens, we miss each other more when we're apart." STEVE, father of Tim, two years Toddlers and preschoolers 57 Toddlers and preschoolers As your baby becomes a toddler, a whole new world of possibilities opens up for him—and for you as a dad. Touch has always been important, but now communicating verbally with your child takes on a new significance as he builds his vocabulary and comprehension. Words are brain food for him. Bridge to the world With toddlers and preschoolers, there are no off-limits areas for moms and dads. Breastfeeding will probably have ended. The only difference will be who is there most often for your child. Usually it is the mom, and the struggle for you to make time doesn't get any easier. But your absence at work shouldn't become a negative thing. It helps you, researchers have reported, to bring distinctive qualities into the home and into the lives of your children. Some studies, for example, suggest that fathers help particularly in developing their child's social skills. This is partly because, during working hours, you are out there in the outside world. In one major survey, preschool children who had spent more time playing with their dads were found to be more sociable when they entered nursery school. You can be a bridge to the outside world. It's clear from everything we know about families that children— especially boys—get a lot out of being around their fathers. Something different from and complementary to what mothers provide takes place at these times. The secret is to define it and to try to repeat it. Cooking together "Dad time" usually revolves around activities, so there is some talking and listening, but only in the background of a shared activity. Often, for conversation to flow, the activity must be able to sustain your child's interest. If it's just an excuse for you to have a heart-to-heart, your child will know this and quickly wander off or clam up. Washing the car can be a great favorite, although it reinforces the stereotype of men and cars. Cooking together can be a good way of breaking tine mold. Even if you re Making time If you feel you're missing out on raising your child, you might consider some of tire options other dads have taken successfully. • Work part-time and decreasing the family's spending Children value your time and attention more than a big house, a big car, and expensive vacations. • Go freelance You can set up an office at home and organize your own timetable so you are around more often during the day. • Get out of the fast lane Tell your boss that you'll be glad to work regular hours but don't want to put in overtime in order to be promoted. • Consider a job-share Working moms do it, so why not dads? There will be financial implications, but also benefits. • Stay at home In increasing numbers, couples are deciding that the dad will stay at home and the mom will go out to work. 58 Being a dad Checklist Follow these guidelines when it comes to disciplining your toddler. • Do make your demands simply and dearly. • Do say "because I say so" when you've run out of alternatives. • Do give more praise than criticism. Be specific with your praise: "Thank you for picking up your toys." • Do reserve any scolding for when you are out of earshot of others. • Don't use put-downs. • Don't compare your child with another "better" one. • Don't try to guilt-trip him about how hard life is for you. • Don't humiliate him by criticizing him in front of other children. hopeless in the kitchen, you will be able to follow a simple cake recipe better than a three-year-old and so win his admiration. If the cake is a flop, turn it into a mutual joke. And if all else fails, get a box of cake mix from the supermarket so that half the hard work is already done before you start. It doesn't matter what it is you're doing as long as the opportunity is there for closeness just to happen, for your conversation to wander into deeper realms, for questions and concerns to pop out of his mouth, for you to be able to influence him in a positive way. Let it go There are two factors to bear in mind when choosing your "dad activity" with your toddler. • Don't expect to complete what you've started. It's the doing, not the finishing, that counts. If an end result is important, wait until he (inevitably) wanders off to find mom and you can complete it on your own. DON'T MISS OUT As your baby reaches the milestones of toddlerhood, make sure you are there to share in his achievements. • Make a choice between your standards and your child. For example, if you’re gardening together, accept that you probably won't end up with a neat row of seedlings in the flower bed after your child helps you plant the seeds. If that's what you want, you should find another activity to do with your toddler. Toddlers and preschoolers 59 A MASCULINE JOB Staying at home to bring up children is becoming an increasingly acceptable and respected male role. Stay-at-home dads Although numbers remain tiny, more and more men are deciding to put being a parent ahead of their careers and opting to stay at home and care for their children. Some men have partners who earn more than they do, so it makes more sense for them to do this. Others do it because they want to. They report that it is deeply satisfying, although there may be some social isolation to overcome. Moms may be getting used to stay-at-home dads, but our ongoing preoccupation with gender makes them nervous about inviting "house- husbands" over for coffee while the children play. And male friends may tease you for being unmasculine, but it's hard to think of anything more masculine than being a good father. Single dads Single dads usually fall into two main categories: the bereaved and the divorced. Whatever the reasons, the number of households in which children live mainly with their father is increasing, and reveals a growing social and legal awareness that a single father can be just as able, loving, and effective in bringing up children as a single mother. Being a single dad isn't easy, but developing a support network of friends, relatives, community organizations, and healthcare professionals can give you practical and emotional support. Your child's pediatrician is a good place to start; he or she may be able to put you in touch with other single dads in your area. Questions & Answers As a child, my dad was the one who handed out the discipline. I don't want to fall into that role, but when my toddler is running riot, I can feel myself heading in that direction. How do I avoid this? Your own upbringing inevitably has an impact on your ideas of parenting, but don't automatically use your own father as a model for your parenting style. Discipline is important, but you must find ways that work for you and for your child. Talk to your partner and come up with a strategy that you both apply equally. Should I be disciplining my toddler, or is it too early to worry about it? No, it's not too early. Your child needs to start developing inner controls and learning how to negotiate and get along with others. Positive example is the biggest part of this, but discipline can back it up. What do I do when my toddler just will not do what I ask him to? Try to stay calm, even if others are watching. Take your child gently to a quiet spot away from the scene of the conflict. If he won t move, kneel down next to him and use a soft, reasonable voice. Explain why you are asking him to do something, and ask him to think about what he is doing and why he is doing it. With many children, this diffuses a potential conflict. I have lost my temper and shouted at my toddler. Now I feel guilty. Is this healthy? All of us crack at some stage. No parent is perfect, however they may appear. Don't be too tough on yourself. If you feel yourself boiling over, take time out. Go to another part of the room where you can keep an eye on your child and wait until your frustration has subsided. 60 Being a dad How can I avoid being a weekend dad? As the role of fathers has changed and their desire has grown to be ever more involved as equal co-parents with their partners in the upbringing of their children, society, lawmakers, and employers have struggled to keep up. Today, millions of fathers are being turned into weekend dads because of a culture of long working hours in our society. So how do you avoid becoming a weekend dad? Know your rights Family leave policies that include a father's right to take time off from work in order to spend time with a newborn and support his partner vary from place to place. Some policies are more generous than others. Find out what the law is in your area and then speak with your employer about taking time off. Stand your ground Rights are one thing, demanding them another. Male colleagues may tease you or resent the time off you get when they are still working hard at their desks or workstations. Managers may question your commitment to your career. If you really want to be there for your children, you need to be a committed advocate. Explain that you can have two loyalties— to work and to family—and that it is all about balance. Be prepared for adverse comments. WORKING AT HOME If you work at home at least some of the time, you will inevitably be around your children much more than if you work in an office five days a week. Avoid guilt At times, you may feel you're being torn in two— between home and work, your partner and your career, being a dad and making financial provisions for your family. Some feelings of guilt may enter into the equation. Try to resist it at all costs so that it does not diminish either side of your life. Push for the best work/life balance you can achieve, but don't beat yourself up if it's not perfect. GETTING INVOLVED Taking a career break to stay home and care for your child will give you a chance to be more involved in her life. Consider the alternatives If your employers really are making it tough for you to be the kind of dad you want to be, consider the alternatives (see page 57). A growing number of men take a career break and stay at home while their partners go out to work. They report that it is deeply satisfying. Other alternatives include stepping off the promotional ladder, working part-time, or working freelance so you can choose your own hours. 62 Being a dad Useful contacts UNITED STATES American Coalition for Fathers and Children 1718 M Street NW, #187 Washington, DC 20056 (800) 978-5237 www.acfc.org Information and services for fathers. ISBN 0-7566-0566-0 Reproduced by Colourscan, Singapore Printed by Star Standard, Singapore Discover more at www.dk.com Foreword 3 A message to parents from The most precious gift in the world is a new baby. Our baby products help mothers and fathers soothe, comfort, and nurture a deep, loving bond with their child through everyday care. Building on our commitment to children and families, Johnson & Johnson established the Johnson & Johnson Pediatric Institute, LLC. This unique organization promotes continued learning and research in paediatrics, infant development, and pregnancy, building programmes and initiatives for professionals, parents, and caregivers that shape the future of children’s health worldwide. Through science, we continue to learn more about our youngest and their physical, cognitive, and emotional development. Parents and caregivers want advice on how to use this learning in their daily lives to complement their basic instincts to love, hold, and talk to their babies. Good parenting is not a one-size-fits-all formula. With JOHNSON'S® Child Development series, we hope to support today’s families with the knowledge, guidance, and understanding to help them bring forth the miracle embodied in each and every child. Ses The beginning of your child's second year is the beginning of a more independent phase, as ‘your baby becomes a toddler. Learning to walk and talk opens up his world, and with you as his guide there is much to explore and discover about his surroundings, his family and friends, and himself, Every day there will be many new experiences to share and enjoy. 6 The second year Your child’s development You have spent the first year learning to understand and meet your baby's physical and emotional needs, and it's been a very hands-on process. Now the focus changes. This second year is much more about helping your toddler become a self-sufficient individual, branching out into the wider world, with you as a guide. Your toddler continues to need your active encouragement to explore her capabilities and her surroundings. She will also need you to return to as a safe emotional base because, for all her apparent independence, she needs your love and rea SSUTrANCE. Developmentally the physical change is enormous. Once your child learns to walk, her horizo ns expand. Re & e es) ag es RS a And learning to talk opens up her world to you, and the whole world to her, in a new and exciting way. Your toddler will constantly attempt to move ahead of her immediate capabilities, which may lead to enormous frustration for her. Learning about limits, her own and those set by you, is new for both of you. With patient teaching and encouragement, she can learn to follow basic safety rules and cooperate with your expectations. Establishing a safe environment As a baby, your toddler explored things with her hands and this continues, except now the exploration isn't limited to those toys given to her. She can move around her home, and everything is worth investigating, whether it's the dog’s bowl, the kitchen cupboards, or the CD player. How can she tell the difference between those buttons she can press and those she can't? It's not possible without your help, so remove items that can be damaged and direct her attention to activities that take advantage of her natural curiosity and pleasure of exploration. Setting the pace for your toddler Toddlers cannot self-limit their activity. They tend to move straight from one activity to another without pause and to put every ounce of their energy into each. Your toddler will rely on you to help set the pace, so that she can manage to enjoy activities without overdoing them to the point of exhaustion, which is sometimes where the flash point of frustration ignites into a tantrum. Toddlers still need lots of rest, and most will probably continue to need at least one daytime nap for this year Well-slept and rested toddlers will manage life better than those who are tired. And if your toddler is a poor sleeper at night, don’t be tempted to keep her going all day in the hope that she will sleep continuously through the night. The more tired she is, the less easy she will find it to relax into a good sleep pattern. Ultimately, this is a wonderfully exciting time for you and your toddler, full of new experiences. Understanding what makes your toddler tick, and what her needs are, will help you create those opportunities that bring out the best in her. About this book During this thrilling year of change, your support, encouragement, and love can do more than anything else to help your toddler blossom. Understanding how your toddler develops is vital to helping you tune into her needs and give her what she wants. Section 1 The first half of this book tells you about how your toddler's development will affect both her physical and her emotional needs. For example, why does your 20- month-old keep having tantrums in public places when previously she was well behaved? How important is it that she talks in simple sentences at a certain age? Now she has begun walking, how can you keep her safe? Being one step ahead in terms of knowing what to expect from your toddler will help you understand her so you can respond in the most effective way possible. And being able to meet her needs in this way will not only help her feel loved and valued but boost your confidence as a parent, too. At this age safety is so important. This book helps you to prepare a safe environment for your child's continuing development. It discusses how to balance safety issues with allowing your toddler the freedom to explore. Section 2 The second half of this book contains what you need to know about how and when your toddler is likely to reach each new milestone. Although the information is organized month by month, it's important to remember that the time-scale is flexible. All toddlers develop at different rates, and your toddler will progress at the speed that’s right for her. Once you see your toddler trying to do something new, there are lots of things you can do to try to encourage her along the way, and this section includes ideas for games and activities you can play with her. Giving your toddler the right kind of stimulation at just the right time will build her confidence and self-esteem and help give her the best possible start in life. 8 The second year Family life The commitment and unconditional love provided by a family will ensure that a toddler has the best possible start in life. Now, a year after he was born, your toddler may still be the newest member of the family, but he is also very much a personality in his own right, beginning to forge his own independent relationships with other family members. Sibling relationships During this second year of your toddler's life you may be having another baby, and this will be a major but positive change in your toddler's life. Your toddler may feel hardly more than a baby himself to you, and you may wonder how he will cope with a new addition. He will take his lead from you, but keep it simple. Don't overplay the benefits of having a brother or sister because it will be some time before they will be able to play together. What he is likely to be most aware of after the new baby arrives is that he won't always be the only one who needs attention. Given that developmentally he is naturally very self-focused, this will take some adjustment on his part. His routine will also be changed. Give him time to adjust, and make sure he still gets some one-to-one time; otherwise his sense of fairness will be Family life 9 offended too! “Role conflict" may also be a problem for a while, as your toddler gets used to no longer being the “baby” of the family. If you already have older children, or stepchildren, then the relationship between them and their younger sibling will become even stronger, even if there are squabbles along the way. Many children seem to fight endlessly, but they are, in fact, forming deep emotional attachments and will probably be great friends and allies as adults. In some ways, children get into a habit of communicating by squabbling, so you will need to set some ground rules so they play together harmoniously. Often an older child will be too “helpful” to his younger sibling. It is frustrating for a toddler who is trying to do something by himself to have someone more competent keep taking his game over. In such a case you may need to point out gently to the older child that the younger child needs more time. However, try not to be too interventionist - your children sometimes need to sort things out between them in their own way. Position in the family Numerous studies have been undertaken to understand if birth order has an impact on personality. If your toddler is your first child, you will probably have had more time to spend with him than is ever going to be likely with any subsequent children. However, with first children there is so much for parents to learn about their care and development, which becomes second nature with later children. First-born children tend to be more achievement-orientated, and are often more strong-willed than later children. They have had the unique experience of never having to share their parents’ attention, at least for a while, and often have a strong sense of responsibility. Second and subsequent children often have better social skills because they have always had to share time and attention with another child, and have sometimes had to take a back seat. They also have to learn to manage living with an older child who will always be more competent than they are. While this may be very frustrating, it may allow them to develop other ways to survive unequal competition. Only children are often very successful in later life because they have had their parents’ undivided attention, and been able to focus on their achievements without having to share with siblings. Twins or more It is important in the case of multiples to try to spend time individually with each baby. This may be a challenge at first, when the physical care of more than one baby takes up so much time. Enlist the help of another family member, or a childminder, to allow you the time and opportunity to do this. | There are two types of twins: identical and non- | identical. The incidence of non-identical multiples has increased in frequency with the use of new fertility treatments. Those children born as a twin or triplet will always have to share. Non-identical or fraternal twins are no more alike than non-twin siblings, but identical twins — who have identical genetic material — will be very similar, although their developing personalities will differ. 10 The second year Emotional development Family life is an important arena for emotional development. You will already be familiar with the development of your baby’s emotions over the first year. From a very early age your baby learned to express pleasure by smiling, Faced with a surprise or completely unknown situation, she may have shown fear by crying. Secure in your arms, she will have settled calmly and happily, expressing contentment. Some children are emotionally very responsive, and others less so. Something that one child finds frightening, is merely of interest to another. During the first year of your child's life, you will have learned a lot about how she approaches the world and you will have been able to help create a balance for her between what she can cope with on her own and with what she needs help. Some babies are easily overstimulated and become fretful, needing more calm and soothing tactics than others. Others are more reticent and will need more encouragement to interact or respond to stimuli. Expressing emotions in security Your child's love for you is easily expressed. She may return your cuddles and kisses with great pleasure, but will also use you to demonstrate stronger emotions like anger. Often for children the development of a full range of emotions can be almost overwhelming, and can only be expressed within a secure environment. You are that secure environment, and in order to experience strong emotions she will need you to help her manage them because she isn’t yet able to do so for herself. You will learn what is best for your child, and it is your role to learn from her cues. Sometimes when Emotional development 11 children are angry, it may be beneficial to hold them in order to help them contain their feelings, talking calmly all the while. Some children respond better to being left alone until they feel better. But, after any emotional outburst, all toddlers need to be reassured with a loving cuddle. The role of imaginative play Apart from the immediate expression of emotions such as happiness, fear, and anger, which are relatively straightforward and easy to recognize in your child, she will begin to imitate expressions of love and concern for others. Being encouraged to demonstrate expressions of affection or sympathy for others, even if she doesn't actually feel it yet, helps with the development of these feelings of empathy. She may also act out different emotions with her teddies or dolls, practising them through her play. This is very important because it means she can experience difficult feelings in a safe place through her imaginative play and begin to understand what it is like to consider other people's feelings. Relating to others What you will notice during the course of this year is that your toddler's pleasure and appreciation of events will begin to include other people. Her excitement at going to a parent and toddler group, for example, will start to reflect her enjoyment and enthusiasm for spending time with particular friends. She may enjoy going to Granny's or visiting another family member because she is developing a close and loving relationship, independent of you, with that person. All these experiences are helping her to develop a full and satisfying emotional life, where she can express her feelings in the safe context of knowing that she is loved and that they are validated. You can make her feel secure no matter what emotions she is expressing. ACTING OUT EMOTIONS This toddler is pretending her much-loved soft toy monkey, Timmy, is tired and needs to have a nap. She puts him to sleep on his back, and makes soothing noises to quieten him ready for sleep. Managing separation Jn eT ERE DOI ERT RESTON TO a nln sail abarin a nN MLnnON da Allowing your child to develop other relationships — with relatives or childminders - independently of you is very beneficial and will help her manage separation from you. Many toddlers are still showing separation | anxiety at this age, and every child will experience it at some point. So take it slowly. Start by playing simple games, such as peekaboo, to help her to understand that things that go away will come back. You can help your toddler believe that she can manage without you for a while by providing her with the experience of doing so. Encourage her to spend time with other loved adults away from home as well as at home. Suggest that she take along a favourite toy | or security object for extra reassurance. Even if she | finds it hard at first, it will help her self-confidence in | the long run. Above all, try not to convey to her that she is totally dependent on you or to impose on her | your own anxiety about being separated from her. | j H ; j t | | | | H | H i i | a 12 The second year Social development During this second year, your toddler is inclined to see life with himself right at its centre. This egocentricity is essential to establishing the secure self-image that will eventually enable him to extend his consideration to other children and adults. Help him build on his self-image and become more sensitive to other people's needs by ensuring that you meet his needs. A lot of social development happens at home quite naturally within the context of family and friends. And when there are siblings, there will probably be less need for your intervention. It's sometimes helpful to allow siblings to sort out their differences between themselves. This day-to-day social interaction with other children at home is not available to first-born or only children, and needs to be sought elsewhere. Initially, this will be through children of parental friends, visits to the park, and parent and toddler groups. In a group of children lca on See? _—_ ee eae where most are older, some of the problems that arise between toddlers won't come up, and this can be an easier environment in some ways to begin social acclimatization. However, he will begin to work out ways of interacting socially with his peer group when he reaches a pre-school environment next year. Discipline is about teaching your toddler what is expected of her, both within the family and in wider society. It is about setting consistent limits and understanding that your toddler's constant testing of these is part of how she will learn to accept them. It should always be done with love and respect for your toddler. Don't expect too much obedience of your toddler. Remember that she still has lots to learn about good behaviour and consideration of others. What also has to be respected is that a young child cannot always make herself understood, especially when it comes to explaining how she is feeling. Sometimes a child will test the limits when feeling anxious, in which case your toddler will need attention and reassurance, not punishment. Thinking about the world from a toddler's point of view, and being sensitive to situations that might be stressful for your child, helps you to see their behaviour in perspective. For example, it's hard to imagine a chair in context unless you can move around it. This is part of a learning process that the psychologists call “object permanence’, meaning that something continues to exist, even after you can no longer see it. An amazing potential People have always been intrigued about why and how babies learn to speak. In the space of three or four years, children pick up virtually all the essentials of a spoken language, apparently without conscious effort or formal lessons. Anyone who has struggled to learn a second language at school or later in life will find it hard to imagine how they do that. All babies learn language, and they do so at the same rate whether they speak English, Spanish, Tagalog, Gujarati, or French. Language is an innate characteristic of humans, and the potential for it is present in all babies at birth, although exactly what the nature of that potential is remains a puzzle. What we do know is that children learn language so quickly it is clear that they must be born with some kind of mechanism that permits it to happen. The remarkable changes that allow language to develop begin very early in a baby’s life, but language skills keep developing right through to adolescence. Your part in the process At first, your baby can do little more than alert you to her needs by crying, but her brain is ready wired to start making sense of language sounds. What she needs is stimulation, and lots of it, from the people around her. Your attention, interest, and conversation provide everything she needs to get started. Most parents don't really need to be told how to interact with their children. It's likely that you began to do so within minutes of your baby’s birth as you greeted her face-to-face for the first time and welcomed her to the world. However, to understand how children learn to talk, it helps to separate out some of its different elements: these are communication, language, and speech. Beginning to communicate It seems that children are born not just to speak but also to interact with other people—first with their parents but soon with everyone else around them. Long before your baby uses words, she uses cries and gestures to make her meaning clear, and responds to and learns to read the gestures and facial expressions of those who care for her. At first, your interaction with your baby is made up of touching, rocking, smiling, and eye contact—gestures that convey your feelings more effectively than words can. They tell your baby that you love her and are interested in her. She understands emotion long before she can talk. GESTURES Smiles, touch, and eye contact tell your baby you are interested in who she is. Gestures, facial expression, and body language are a major part of communication in these early months and continue to be so throughout life. Think how much you use them to enhance your speech and interpret what you hear. They are an essential fallback when a meaning is unclear or a language is foreign to you. However, human communication is also about referring to and describing the world, and this is the next step your child takes toward becoming a talker. Once she has established what words do and how they relate to things, it is only a matter of time before she is naming what she sees— doggy; “car” “milk! or “mom: What is language? Language in general, and grammar in particular, is what distinguishes humans from other animals. Our system of combining words into meaningful sequences enables us to give shape to our ideas and thoughts and convey them to others. One of the really distinctive features of our capacity to learn language is our ability to be creative with sentences. Although we use some expressions Over and over again, we are constantly producing new sentences that we have never said before and that we have never heard anyone else say, either. In teaching programs, some have learned to use hundreds of signs and understand even more. However, even the cleverest gorillas and chimpanzees are able to form only the most basic sentences. By two-and-a-half, most children are using the three main components of a complex language system. They learn the rules of phonology as they combine sounds into words. Then they get to grips with syntax as they combine words in the correct order to make up phrases and sentences such as “Get ball" or “Juice all gone’ Although these are simple requests and observations, they are semantic (they have a precise meaning). Children's language skills are not simply confined to what they are able to say—they also need to understand what they hear. An essential part of learning to talk is using what they know about language to work out what others are saying. 10 Learning to talk When does learning to talk begin? A baby’s first experiences with sounds begin in the womb. In the last weeks of pregnancy, the pathways in the brain that allow hearing are already well developed, and babies begin to recognize sounds they hear often, especially their mother’s voice. They sometimes kick strongly in response to a loud noise or become still when soft music is played. Fascinating research Babies in the womb can learn to recognize a wide range of sounds—even a story, if it is read to them often enough. In one study, a group of newborns showed that they could recognize Dr. Seuss’ The Cat in the Hat after their mothers read the story aloud twice a day during the last six weeks of pregnancy. In another study, newborns responded to the theme tune of a soap opera their mothers watched every day. No one suggests that babies can learn to talk in the womb, but research shows that they are equipped to start learning from you at birth. After birth Once your baby is born, the process of learning to talk is closely linked to her social development. She must want to communicate, and this may not be automatic in all children. In most cases, what makes your baby want to talk is you. SOUNDS BEFORE BIRTH Toward the end of your pregnancy, try playing a piece of music to your baby every day during a quiet moment. You may find she is soothed by it after the birth. The miracle of speech 11 FACE TO FACE Your face, your smile, and the sound of your voice mean everything to your young baby. Watching and listening to you speak and making her own sounds in response puts her on the path to becoming a talker herself. ¥% At first, she is fascinated by your face and gazes at your eyes and mouth while you make the sounds she likes so much. She uses body language and smiles to show that she is pleased to see you. %* Next, she has to listen for the sounds of speech all around her and start trying them out herself. Then she has to make associations between the sounds that we call words and what they refer to. This means that, at the very least, she must be able to remember what she has seen and heard. ¥% Becoming mobile is often the final spur to speech because it broadens her experience. Now she has so much more to tell you, she has an even greater drive to communicate. She becomes able to make speech sounds as her larynx descends and her pharynx lengthens. This is happening rapidly by the end of her first year and is complete by age three. Making speech sounds is not an easy task for a baby and relies as much on her physical development as her growing ability to think. She has to be able to control her head, bring her lips together deliberately, move her tongue up and down, and use the soft palate at the top of her mouth to produce them. All of this has to be coordinated with her breathing and the movement of her voice box (larynx). Do children have to learn language at a particular stage in their life, and is the chance lost forever if they are not given enough stimulation? No scientist would prevent a child from learning language, so answers to these questions have to be based on rare examples of children who have been raised in isolation with no meaningful contact with humans. From these studies, it appears that a child who is not exposed to language in the first eight or nine years is very unlikely to learn language. Although language learning is innate, it appears to rely on experiences during key periods for its development. What is certain is that the first three years of life are a critically important learning period for children. The drive to communicate Your newborn baby may seem like a small, helpless bundle, but he is an active communicator from day one. At first, his cries and burps relate only to how he is feeling, whether he is hungry, tired, needs a clean diaper, or has gas. Although he doesn't yet know that he is sending out a message, your response teaches him that his cries have consequences— they bring rewards. It’s not long before he begins to use crying to express specific needs and focus it on the people who are likely to do something about them. He is already beginning to communicate. Your first conversations are all about kindness, reassurance, and making him feel safe. Most parents chatter away to their babies without really being aware of it: “Hello, baby, did you wake up for your feeding?" “Over to Daddy, now—he wants to change your diaper’ “Ooh, you don't want me to take off your T-shirt, do you?" To your baby, this is nothing more than a meaningless string of sounds, but they make him feel calm and attended to nonetheless. As soon as he is born, they help him to know who and what is important to him, and gradually, over the coming months, he is trained to use his senses to gather information. Even if he can hear, he must learn to listen. As soon as he can focus, he needs to learn to direct his attention so he can begin to recognize gestures, facial expressions, familiar objects, and movements. In these first few weeks, hold him just a short distance from your face as you talk to him so he can focus on your eyes and lips. If you call out to him and talk reassuringly when he begins to cry, he may pause momentarily and be calmed by your voice. Loud noises such as a door slamming may alarm him; he freezes all his limbs and then breaks into a distraught wail. When he smiles back, it is like a magic ingredient that makes everything work better, especially if your first few weeks with a new baby have been an uphill battle. At first, your baby’s fleeting imitations of smiles have not really been under his control nor related to anything in particular; however, by six weeks, his smile is less automatic and he prefers faces to any other visual treat. Making comparisons Speech and language development is such an obvious part of.a child's growing up that it is one of the most common areas in which parents seek reassurance. Knowing what to expect can be difficult, however, if you have little experience of children other than your own, and if you do make comparisons with other children, you are likely to focus on the most proficient talkers rather than the range of accomplishments across your child's age group. Your own parents may also make comparisons across the generations that cannot always be relied upon. Like adults, children find some activities easier than others, and although their development tends to follow the same sequence, the exact age at which skills develop differs from one child to the next. Each new skill develops within a broad period; whether your child masters it early or late within the time span, she can still be considered to be developing normally. Ask him to bring his shoes, socks, pants, coat, etc. e 3-4 years Ask your child to act out instructions using toys. Include a mix of words such as “fast” and “slow,” “under” and “over,” “in” | and “out.” For example, “Now your spider crawls under the pillow...” e 4-5 years Show pictures of animals and household objects and pose questions: “Which animals climb trees?" “What do we use when we want to cook bacon and eggs?” 54 Learning to talk = Expert tips If your child is 18 months to two years old, try this test to check how well she coordinates her lips and tongue—a necessary skill for speaking words. Give her a dry, crumbly cookie and watch how she eats it. e Does she bite off small bits and deal with each in turn, or-does she stuff the whole thing into her mouth? e Does she leave crumbs around her mouth, or is she able to coordinate her lips and tongue to lick them off? e If she misses some crumbs on her face and you draw her attention to them, can she then lick them off? Some children do not manage to pronounce these sounds correctly until around the age of eight. A lisp is often caused by a tooth problem because, to produce a clear /s/ sound, a child needs to be able to expel air through a tiny gap between her teeth. Gaps or missing teeth can make pronunciation difficult, as can wearing orthodontic braces later on. Most children manage these trickier sounds eventually as they develop the muscles they need for speech, but if problems persist, a speech therapist can show your child how to position her tongue and lips while she practices the sounds. CHECKING DEVELOPMENT Use your child’s regular developmental checks to talk through concerns with your healthcare provider. Looking at the whole child Speech is often a focus of parents’ concern, but it is important to look at all aspects of a child's development because difficulties often occur together. General learning difficulties are the most common source of speech and language difficulties. A child who is slow to start doing all sorts of things, such as crawling, walking, and feeding herself, is likely to develop language and speech slowly, too. Depending on the severity of a child's difficulties, this need not be a problem as long as her parents and teachers are aware of her needs and make sure she has support. Checking on progress 55 A language problem Some children, however, have trouble acquiring language even though all their other learning skills are intact. Primary language difficulties (or specific language difficulties) are thought to run in families. Sometimes the problem is that a child simply cannot understand what others are saying. This may be hard to pick up at first because young children often get by using context and visual cues. In other cases, children understand what people say but are unable to form sentences at the right level for their age and thus carry on using gestures instead of speech. They can become very frustrated as they struggle to get their meaning across. Later on, they find it difficult to form past and future tenses, for example, or organize their ideas into stories. They may also go on to have difficulties learning to read and write. A speech difficulty Most children's speech is difficult to understand at times, but those with a specific speech difficulty cannot communicate because they either use too few speech sounds or continue to use the sounds they developed as babies. They know what they want to say but are frustrated because they cannot access the right sounds. Does he need to have speech therapy? Most children stutter occasionally, especially when they are excited and their ideas outstrip their vocabulary. You can help your son by trying not to finish words for him or being impatient or embarrassed when he speaks, and not forcing him to speak when he is nervous. The checklist below will help you decide if your child has a difficulty that is becoming entrenched. If you are concerned, ask for him to be referred for speech and language therapy. e Does he talk normally when he is on his own or with close friends and family? Stuttering may simply be due to anxiety about talking to strangers. e Is he frustrated by his speech and becoming aware that he has a problem? If so, seek professional advice. @ Does he repeat words or parts of words, or show tension and “block” when he starts to speak? Sounds at the beginning of words are often a problem for children who stutter. How can we make sure our twin girls develop speech normally? Twins are often late talkers, partly because they are usually premature or low-birthweight babies, but also because their parents may have less time for individual language activities than parents of single children. It's not uncommon for twins to develop their own language or “idioglossia,” understood only by each other. To avoid problems, try to find opportunities for your twins to speak and act individually. Deciding exactly when your child has reached a point in her language development where she needs help is not always easy. Consider some of the following ideas if you are worried about any aspect of her language and speech. If you are still concerned, see your healthcare provider, who will be able to refer her for expert assessment WATCH AND LISTEN Spending time observing and listening to your child when she is alone with you or with her friends will help you decide if she needs some help with her communication skills, Things to consider %& Make time for your child to have relaxed conversations with you. If she has older siblings, she may not have had quite as much attention as your first child. Does she have an older brother or sister who does the talking for her? % Make sure her daycare or school has sufficient staff for plenty of one-to-one interaction. The “terrible twos" (the period between two and three years of age) is often a time when children begin to assert themselves to show off their new-found independence as well as their physical and language skills. This is also the time when parents learn to adapt their style of management to one that is more reasoned and negotiable. Although this period tests us as parents, it is a perfectly normal phase that most children go through. Some children, however, remain difficult to manage in daycare and through into preschool. When this happens, it is important to think carefully about what might be causing this "naughty" behavior. Is your child being rebellious and willful, or has she not understood what is expected of her? Watch carefully to see what leads up to the episodes of naughtiness. She showed us exactly how she felt, and or “A pitta it wasn t long aun REEMA before she was Ru AONE AP ‘ahs fe bets rab telling us what to do, too.” JOSH, father of Sarah, age three The miracle of speech 7 The miracle of speech Learning to talk is one of the most amazing things that children do—but it happens so automatically you may never give much thought to how your baby accomplishes it, Within a few years, your crying newborn baby becomes an engaging companion asking questions, telling stories, and letting you know exactly how she feels. An amazing potential People have always been intrigued about why and how babies learn to speak. In the space of three or four years, children pick up virtually all the essentials of a spoken language, apparently without conscious effort or formal lessons. Anyone who has struggled to learn a second language at school or later in life will find it hard to imagine how they do that. All babies learn language, and they do so at the same rate whether they speak English, Spanish, Tagalog, Gujarati, or French. Language is an innate characteristic of humans, and the potential for it is present in all babies at birth, although exactly what the nature of that potential is remains a puzzle. What we do know is that children learn language so quickly it is clear that they must be born with some kind of mechanism that permits it to happen. The remarkable changes that allow language to develop begin very early in a baby’s life, but language skills keep developing right through to adolescence. Your part in the process At first, your baby can do little more than alert you to her needs by crying, but her brain is ready wired to start making sense of language sounds. What she needs is stimulation, and lots of it, from the people around her. Your attention, interest, and conversation provide everything she needs to get started. Most parents don't really need to be told how to interact with their children. It's likely that you began to do so within minutes of your baby’s birth as you greeted her face-to-face for the first time and welcomed her to the world. What this book sets out to do is enhance an interaction that comes naturally, to enrich the experience for you both. | and lots of good examples of talk. eee SEN Talking to children matters. | For example, in a recent study, researchers identified a noticeable decline in language skills in three- year-olds in the UK. They believe that many children are starting preschool without ever having had one-to-one conversations. The concern is that parents are not spending enough time talking ' to their children, possibly because | they are relying too much on toys, television, and computer games | that entertain without adult / interaction. To become able talkers, | children need one-to-one practice 8 Learning to talk The basics of talk Most of the time we communicate so effortlessly, we fail to appreciate how complex human communication is. However, to understand how children learn to talk, it helps to separate out some of its different elements: these are communication, language, and speech. Beginning to communicate It seems that children are born not just to speak but also to interact with other people—first with their parents but soon with everyone else around them. Long before your baby uses words, she uses cries and gestures to make her meaning clear, and responds to and learns to read the gestures and facial expressions of those who care for her. At first, your interaction with your baby is made up of touching, rocking, smiling, and eye contact—gestures that convey your feelings more effectively than words can. They tell your baby that you love her and are interested in her. She understands emotion long before she can talk. GESTURES
