GARTH, father of Jane, three weeks The birth 17 The birth The birth of your child is a major event in your life. It is the end of the waiting after nine months and the start of a new life, the formal beginning of a relationship, the first page of a lifelong story. Many men now choose to be present at the births of their children. Your role But what is your role during birth, and who are you there for—yourself, your partner, or your newborn child? The answer should be "all three." You are witnessing part of your own history. You are supporting the person closest to you as she goes through what can be a difficult physical and emotional experience to give birth to the child you have both created and nurtured. And you are welcoming a new member of your family. For many men it is a deeply moving, almost miraculous event, but it can also be distressing if you see your partner in pain, or if you don't understand what is happening if medical complications set in. Playing your part In order to play a full role, make sure you understand the mechanics of birth. You will be of little use to your partner if you have to keep asking her or the doctor or midwife what is happening. You should also take time to talk through with your partner how she wants to handle the birth and pain relief. She may have written down a birth plan (see below). When she's in the middle of the emotions of labor, she will rely on you to make her wishes plain to her healthcare providers. And, in advance of the event, consider realistically how you are going to handle your own emotions and fears about witnessing the birth of your child. The birth plan Doctors and midwives often advise couples to write down a birth plan before their baby is due to be born. Circumstances may intervene, but it enables you to approach labor with a clear view of how you both would like it to proceed. Since it is your partner who will go through the Expert tips There are several good reasons for being at the birth of your child: • because it is a life-changing experience to see your child born • to support your partner • to help her communicate with healthcare providers | • to welcome your child. physical experience of labor, hers must be the guiding voice. Try to stay open-minded, however. This is only a rough guide, and once labor begins, your partner may change her mind about some of the plans. A written birth plan should cover the following areas: • who will attend the birth • your partner's views on induction • what pain relief she wants • what position she would like to be in for labor 18 Being a dad WRITING A BIRTH PLAN Writing a birth plan with your partner helps you both to be clear on what her wishes are once labor starts. Checklist The following are things you'll need to have ready to take to the hospital: plenty of change (remember, you can't use a cell phone in the hospital, so you will have to use the pay phone); a list of telephone numbers of key relatives and friends; some drinks and snacks, since it may be a long time before you have a chance to go to the hospital cafeteria; a camera for the first shot of your newborn child. Your partner's bag should include: nightgowns and a bathrobe; two maternity bras; breast pads; sanitary pads; several pairs of underpants (either cotton or disposable); clothes to go home in; toiletries (toothbrush and toothpaste, washcloth, towel, hairbrush, shampoo, lotion, makeup). For your baby you will need: diapers and baby wipes; onesies or sleepers; a sweater or coat and a hat to go home in; a blanket; a car seat. • what position she would like to be in for birth • what medical procedures she will consent to during birth • what she would like tire medical staff to do with the baby as soon as it arrives (hand it straight to you, for example) • her attitude to breastfeeding • thoughts on possible birth complications, such as emergency cesareans or intervention to speed up labor. The birth 19 What will happen Whether you and your partner have decided on a home birth or a hospital delivery, you will be joined at the birth by at least one healthcare provider. If it is a home birth, you may well find yourself playing a practical role as assistant midwife. In the hospital, in addition to the nursing staff, there will usually be doctors present. They will all be eager for you to participate as fully as possible in the birth. Being a supporter We naturally defer to doctors, so it may be tempting to play along and adopt a background role by leaving your partner in "expert hands." But if you want it, there is a vital role for you as your partner's supporter and advocate. She will be able to see you, the father of the child soon to be born, amid potentially unfamiliar medical faces. She may want to discuss with you the professional advice she is getting from her healthcare providers and compare it with the birth plan that you have worked out together beforehand. There may be occasions when what seems to the medical staff to be the best way forward doesn't quite match up with what \ your partner feels her body ( is telling her. Listen to what your partner is saying. Support her in her choices and politely but firmly pass on any views or concerns she wants to communicate to the hospital staff. The experience of seeing the one you love in pain can be disconcerting, but pain, you must remember, is a natural part of childbirth. Your protective instinct may make you want to force the medical staff to administer pain relief, but stop for a moment and weigh this against what your partner has decided in her birth plan. Resist the urge to try to take over. Recognize the uniqueness of the situation and make sure you keep a level head. Three stages of labor The first stage: the cervix opens up (dilates) to allow the baby's head to pass through. Contractions thin, soften, and stretch the cervix. Dilation is measured in centimeters, up to a maximum of around 10. This can be a long process, especially with a first labor. The second stage: this is shorter, usually no more than two hours. Your partner will feel a reflex to push down during contractions. Gradually the baby's head will appear, leading to delivery. The third stage: this lasts from delivery until the uterus contracts again to expel the placenta— usually after 15 minutes or so. A SUPPORTING ROLE Rubbing your partner's back will help ease the pain as she copes with contractions. 20 Being a dad Ways to help during labor Labor can be a very lengthy process, and while your partner is in the midst of it, there will be many ways in which you can help and encourage her: • rubbing her back to ease the pain caused by the contractions • supporting her weight as she adopts some of the pain-relieving positions learned in prenatal classes • wiping her forehead • encouraging her and even joining her in breathing exercises • providing a steady supply of drinks and, if she wants it, energy¬ giving food • putting on soothing music • distracting her from tine pain by reading, talking, or playing games • feeling and timing her contractions • filling in insurance forms. Safety valve There may be times during labor when your partner's pain is such that she just has to let off steam and shout at someone. She may do it with the medical staff. They have plenty of experience with women in labor and will know how to handle this. Be prepared, too, for her to shout at you. Respond calmly with soothing words of praise and encouragement. She is only taking it out on you because she loves you and knows that she can. After the birth Once your baby has been delivered, a nurse or the midwife will clean him or her up. The baby will be returned to you after a couple of minutes. Usually, while your partner receives further medical attention- removal of the placenta, for example—you will be given your child to hold. It is a moment when it is impossible not to be emotional. Don’t feel shy about letting your feelings out. The medical staff will have seen fathers cry many times before. Your bonding with your child has begun. The medical staff will quickly start to peel away and give you time to be alone with your partner and your child. Don't rush this most precious moment. Your partner may want to The birth 21 talk over the labor with you, or about what you saw and what she experienced. She may also simply want you to join her in gazing in adoration at the tiny boy or girl in front of you. An odd hiatus If the labor has been a complicated one, or if your partner has had a cesarean, she may have to stay in the hospital to recover. You will be tired and feel tempted to go home and sleep. Don't feel bad about this. Your energy will be needed in abundance soon enough. If you have other children, they will need your special love and attention during a time that may be challenging for them. Questions & Answers Should I watch as the baby emerges from my partner's body? This is something you can discuss with your partner before the birth, but once you are both caught up in the labor, your feelings may change. For some men, it is part of the most extraordinary thing they will ever witness, and watching helps in the bonding process with their child. For others, the sight during a natural birth of what had previously been an intimate part of their partner's body in such a raw state may be disturbing. You will have a strong instinct which way to go when you are in the labor room. My wife wants to watch the baby coming out. How can I help? You can position and hold a mirror that will enable her to watch as she pushes. Whatever you do, don't get in the way of the hospital staff and don't offer a running commentary unless asked. Your partner will be preoccupied with what her body is going through and she doesn't need any distractions. What should I do when the baby first comes out? The medical staff usually places the baby, still attached by its umbilical cord, on your partner's body so she can see and hold the new arrival. Some couples find it soothing for the man at this stage to put his arms around both mother and child. It keeps them warm and signals that the three of you are a unit. Can I cut the umbilical cord? If the birth has been straightforward, there will be no medical objection to your doing this. Modern practice is to do it within the first 10 to 15 minutes after birth. It is another way of feeling part of the process, but it may not be for the squeamish. 22 Being a dad How can I bond with my newborn? By the end of the first week, given sufficient exposure to you, your baby will recognize you and your smell, and you will already begin to get a sense of the personality that is unfolding before you. By six weeks there will be smiles; by 12 weeks, chuckles. The bonding process is all about love, acceptance, and celebration. For your partner, especially if she is breastfeeding, there is a natural hormonal bonding impetus. The baby needs feeding and she is the one who can do it. For you, die routes to bonding are different, but no less instinctive. Touch and sound Hold your baby. If your partner is breastfeeding she will probably take on die majority of the childcare in the first few weeks, but retreating into housekeeping and domestic chores isn't the sum total of your role. Take every chance you can to pick up and cuddle your child. Dads who care for babies physically start to get fascinated and very in tune with them. This is called engrossment. Time If at first your baby doesn't settle easily with you and wants your partner, take it in stride. You will get the hang of it. Because you cannot give the immediate comfort of breast milk, it may take you a Me time to learn how to meet your child's needs. Be confident and work your way through different ways of calming until you discover the right ones. HOLDING AND CUDDLING Pick up your baby and cuddle her every time you get a chance, and the bonding process will simply happen almost without your being aware of it. FUNNY FACES Make time to do nothing but watch your baby. Get to know her range of little movements and savor the amazing array of funny faces she makes, especially when she's asleep. Euphoria Amid the chaos of the first weeks with a small baby, try to maintain a sense of the sheer wonder of being a father, of having created new life, and of nurturing that life. Make time to watch your baby while she sleeps, see her eyes scrunching up, twitching in the middle of dreams, her little fists clenching and unclenching, her arms reaching out and stretching before she falls back into a deep sleep. These magical moments, which you can savor, will all help strengthen the bonds forming between you. PRACTICAL BONDING Although you can't breastfeed your new baby, there are other practical things you can do that will help you bond with her—diaper¬ changing being a fine example! " I went into parenthood with my eyes wide open but it has exceeded my expectations so much that it is all the harder to juggle my work and my home life." PHILIP, father of Rowan, three months What is a dad's role? 25 What is a dad's role? The i ole of fathers has come under more sustained scrutiny in recent times than ever before. This is partly because of the evolution in women's roles in society in the developed world. As women increasingly seek career opportunities outside the home, should that leave dad holding the baby? What's right for you As a response to such questions, we are now bombarded with media images of fathers—be they the lone dads of Hollywood movies, the weekend dads created by the ever- increasing demands of the workplace, or the dads trying and often failing to juggle all their responsibilities in the modern two-income family. Which of these composites fits your life? Probably none. Each of us has to cope with our circumstances as best we can and attempt, in consultation with our partner, to forge our own model of fatherhood. Co-parenting At one time, the idea of fathering was seen principally in its biological context—literally begetting a child. Mothering, by contrast, included the notion of caring and nurturing. As a simple, relaxing, and effective way of bonding, cuddling up and enjoying a book together is difficult to beat. Never too early Some experts believe you should start reading to babies while they are still in the womb, but it will be in the second half of the first year that your child can become an active participant in the reading process—if only by chewing the corners of the books you are reading to her! The rhythm and sound of the words rather than their meanings will be the first things to make an impact, followed by the colors, patterns, and shapes in the illustrations. Tone of voice Tone and inflection are key components when you read aloud to your child. Don't imagine you are speaking to an adult audience from a podium or presenting the news on television. If you need prompting as to what catches a child's attention, tune in to a children's TV program and listen to the presenters' style of delivery. Make your voice sing-song, not monotonous; add exaggerated emphasis; and repeat yourself to convey the detail. If what you are reading is funny, laugh out loud and then watch your child imitate you. READING TOGETHER Looking at books together and reading to your child will help her develop a love of books that she will retain throughout her life. she will make sense of the world, overcome her fears, and learn to relate to others. • Face to face Design your games around staying in face-to-face contact. Our faces are the most expressive part of us and the most obvious channel for communicating the love and information that will help your baby grow. • Rough-and-tumble Make as much noise as you like, and incorporate suitable elements of rough-and-tumble into your play. Dads can have a special role in nurturing the physical aspect of their children's development. Landmarks Even the most mundane activity can be turned into a treat for your child if you have the right attitude. If it has to be done, you have the choice of making it a chore or making it an adventure. A car ride, for example, can be an occasion for joyous singing and giggles, or you can make a trip to the supermarket a fun time—and shoulder your part of domestic life at the same time. Small children need little encouragement to delight in the bright colors and lights of these consumer temples. A program of child-centered, educational trips and activities is not necessary. With the right attitude TIME OUT When you take your baby out for a walk, interact with her by talking about what you can see—the leaves on the trees and the clouds in the sky, for example. on your part and with your commitment of time, the weekend chores can be the ultimate learning opportunity. Even if you don't feel up to it, be positive and creative. Don't retreat behind the newspaper at breakfast time, but play airplanes with a spoonful of cereal. Don't sit glued to the news on television or stay in bed until noon on Saturday morning. Your child's childhood will pass quickly enough, so make sure you get involved and are a part of it. Sleep time Once your baby has passed the eight-week stage, she should be ready to settle into a sleeping pattern. By a happy coincidence, the most Expert tip 48 Being a dad SHARED CARE Caring for your child is a responsibility you can share with your partner—and like all the other activities you do with your child, it can be bonding, rewarding, and fun. natural time for her to go to sleep— around 7 o'clock in the evening—is also the time that many working dads arrive home. What better way to change gear from breadwinner to nurturing father than to get involved in the going-to-bed ritual and make it your special time. Older siblings As your children get older, the basic patterns of family life will be for you and your partner to share yourselves, both as a couple and as individuals, equally between your children in terms of love, affection, time, outings, and so on. At this early stage, however, your partner may still be breastfeeding, and if you have older children they may feel that their mother’s attention is rather lop-sided in favor of the new arrival. In such a situation, dads can be a great corrective. An older sibling's envying a new brother or sister is perfectly natural. Most big brothers and sisters go through a stage where they want to be a baby again—so they can replace the infant sibling on their mother's lap or even at her breast. Be prepared for some regressive behavior. It isn’t a big deal. Constant requests to "be a good big Bedtime stories work well for dads who are just home from work, but you can, of course, read together at any time. Have books lying around so they are always on hand to fill a spare five minutes or to assist you in distracting or calming an unhappy child. Make books seem normal by having them available, not extraordinary by keeping them high on a shelf out of your child's reach. For very young children, small, sturdy books are best because they let you lay them flat while you read, and your child can help turn the chunky pages. Vinyl books are good for bathtime. Rhymes have a strong appeal to the ears, and books that include activities contribute to making storytime fun. brother/sister" or "set a good example" are not the best policy and can often cause resentment. As tine parent with more freedom and flexibility in these early stages, you can take time to indulge older siblings a little by way of compensation, to praise their grown¬ up attributes, to point out all they can do that the baby can’t, and to reassure them that family life as they have come to know it will soon resume. The arrival of a new baby will inevitably have disturbed your usual routine, lrips and outings may have fallen by the wayside. The first year 49 ROUTINE REQUIREMENTS Developing a bedtime routine and sticking to it will greatly help your child learn to fall asleep easily. Bedtime Here are a few practical tips to help make bedtime easier. • Build up gradually to bedtime with a bath, reading a story, lots of hugs, kisses, and cuddles, then dimming the lights. • Perhaps combine the extended bedtime ritual with a final drink of water from a cup (once your baby is no longer being exclusively breastfed). Don’t worry about establishing a precedent. She will grow out of bedtime drinks naturally later on. • Devote yourself completely to what you're doing (so much so that you could easily fall asleep, too). If your baby senses that you are anxious for her to nod off so that you can get on with other things, she will fight sleep even harder because she doesn't want you to go away. • Keep to your routine and make changes or adjustments gradually. The security that comes from an endlessly repeating process will, in time, aid sleep. Make time to take your older children out, to have fun with them, to give them your full attention, and to listen to their views. Talk positively with them about their new brother or sister and how much they will add to family life once they have grown a little. " I have a great relationship with my daughter, and when my son was born, I wondered how different it would be. I've quickly discovered they both need me just the same." LEE, father of Esther, three years, and Jack, six months Boys and girls 51 Boys and girls Are men more interested in being fathers to sons, and is it the natural role of dads to focus on their sons and moms on their daughters? One organization that runs parenthood seminars reports that in most classes the ratio of men to women is 1 to 4. However, when the topic is raising boys, it is more like 1 to 1. A changing picture In short, the answer to the questions above is "yes" on both counts. We identify with our own sex more easily. Dads know what it's like to grow up as a boy. Part of that is how to develop masculinity, and dads clearly feel, with some justification, that they have much to contribute here, although in their absence, single moms often manage very well. Yet while it may be traditional for dads to concentrate their parenting on boys and moms on girls, that picture is inevitably changing in an age when men's and women's roles in society at large are becoming increasingly interchangeable. Love is all you need It is possible in our postfeminist age to get too tied up with gender. For children, the gender of the parents caring for them is much less important than if they can show warmth and kindness. Parents, meanwhile, love their children for who they are rather than what they are. The key to success as a parent is to be yourself, with your unique cocktail of what are still labeled masculine and feminine qualities. Your children know nothing about labels. They will learn from what you are, not from your gender. Dads are for everyone This is especially true with babies. Babies are babies, not boy babies or girl babies. It doesn't concern them, and we shouldn't worry about it too much, either By toddlerhood, however, boys tend to move around more and occupy more space. In general, they like the more vigorous kind of play that dads can offer. Rough-and-tumble with dad is a special treat and discharges pent-up energy and aggression that accompanies testosterone spurts in these years. Gender differences The differences between boys and girls: • are few compared to their similarities • are only tendencies • don't apply to every individual, or your children • don't have to be accepted by you. Fathering and mothering are not always the same. They are two complementary but ultimately different kinds of input. Dads, for example, are often better at robust play, while moms excel at calming children down. The two sets of skills work together, so having a mother and father present and active in their lives gives children the best chance of growing into happy, well- balanced adults—although they can, of course, reach the same point with solo parents or same sex parents. AVOIDING STEREOTYPES Cooking with your son, no matter what the outcome, can be fun and provide some calm time for talking. Dads and boys In a traditional two-parent family, the principal source of information about masculinity is from the dad. The first thing you need to do is to decide what you feel masculinity is all about so you won't confuse your sons—or, indeed, your daughters. Here are some questions you might like to consider. • How far is masculinity bound up with traditionally "male" interests such as sports, cars, or just "hanging out with the guys"? • How do you reconcile popular images of men being tough with the nurturing role you take on in your home? • How do you show love and affection and still be masculine? • Does your attitude to this differ in private and in public? • Do you care if people—other men in particular—regard you as unmasculine? • How do you feel men should behave toward women? Dads and girls There is, of course, no reason why dads cannot encourage their daughters to be great soccer players or to have high career ambitions. Both parents should avoid male and female stereotypes at this early stage Boys and girls 53 and allow their children room to be their own people. It is the best way of preparing them for the world where equal opportunities are now each individual's right. Gender equality Saying boys are different can easily develop into saying they are not as good as girls. With girls increasingly turning the tables on boys in some SOCCER SKILLS areas of educational achievement, it seems strange to us that previous generations of parents thought that girls were fundamentally different from boys and, for example, could never have careers in industry, science, or business. There is a move now to reestablish equal opportunities for boys and girls, and dads have a special role to play in achieving that goal. Why dads matter Boys growing up with an absentee father are statistically more likely to: • get physically injured • be violent • get into trouble • do poorly at school • be a member of a teenage gang in adolescence. Girls growing up with an absentee father are statistically more likely to: • have low self-esteem • have sex before they're ready • drop out of school. Don't make the assumption that your daughter won't enjoy sports as much as your son—given the opportunity, she will probably be just as enthusiastic. 54 Being a dad How can I be a positive role model? Being a positive role model boils down to setting a good example for your children— both sons and daughters—for life. By offering and demonstrating love, warmth, and kindness, and by taking an active role in their lives, you can show them that men make great dads, and that great dads are great parents. mm Boys and girls 55 HEALTHY OFFERINGS Set a good example for your children by cooking healthy meals for your family. Be a good parent Make fatherhood as natural as it is manly. Express feelings as well as indulging in vigorous activities; earn money and help out at home; teach baseball skills but know how to bake cookies. Be the best advertisement for the joys, achievements, and satisfaction of fatherhood that you can be. Do as I do What they see you do, your children will copy. Just because you have been out at work all day, you are not exempt from following house rules when you are at home. So eating unhealthily, for example, especially when your partner has spent all week coaxing your children off potato chips and onto apples, is not setting a good example. You might also consider that a good diet increases the odds that you will be around later on. Most of the causes of early death in men in the developed world—cancer, heart disease, strokes— are affected by what you eat. Try new hobbies Have a range of interests and hobbies, and be prepared to increase them in search of things you can do with your children. Swimming or cycling, for example, are sports you can do side by side. Encourage your children to widen their horizons by taking the plunge with them in a spirit of adventure. Happy home Be relaxed with your partner in front of your children. Show them how strong your love is for their mother and thus give them reassurance about the basic security of their home life and a positive model of co-parenting for the future. 11 Once Tim started running around, I found it harder to leave him and go out to work. As my relationship with him grows and deepens, we miss each other more when we're apart." STEVE, father of Tim, two years Toddlers and preschoolers 57 Toddlers and preschoolers As your baby becomes a toddler, a whole new world of possibilities opens up for him—and for you as a dad. Touch has always been important, but now communicating verbally with your child takes on a new significance as he builds his vocabulary and comprehension. Words are brain food for him. Bridge to the world With toddlers and preschoolers, there are no off-limits areas for moms and dads. Breastfeeding will probably have ended. The only difference will be who is there most often for your child. Usually it is the mom, and the struggle for you to make time doesn't get any easier. But your absence at work shouldn't become a negative thing. It helps you, researchers have reported, to bring distinctive qualities into the home and into the lives of your children. Some studies, for example, suggest that fathers help particularly in developing their child's social skills. This is partly because, during working hours, you are out there in the outside world. In one major survey, preschool children who had spent more time playing with their dads were found to be more sociable when they entered nursery school. You can be a bridge to the outside world. It's clear from everything we know about families that children— especially boys—get a lot out of being around their fathers. Something different from and complementary to what mothers provide takes place at these times. The secret is to define it and to try to repeat it. Cooking together "Dad time" usually revolves around activities, so there is some talking and listening, but only in the background of a shared activity. Often, for conversation to flow, the activity must be able to sustain your child's interest. If it's just an excuse for you to have a heart-to-heart, your child will know this and quickly wander off or clam up. Washing the car can be a great favorite, although it reinforces the stereotype of men and cars. Cooking together can be a good way of breaking tine mold. Even if you re Making time If you feel you're missing out on raising your child, you might consider some of tire options other dads have taken successfully. • Work part-time and decreasing the family's spending Children value your time and attention more than a big house, a big car, and expensive vacations. • Go freelance You can set up an office at home and organize your own timetable so you are around more often during the day. • Get out of the fast lane Tell your boss that you'll be glad to work regular hours but don't want to put in overtime in order to be promoted. • Consider a job-share Working moms do it, so why not dads? There will be financial implications, but also benefits. • Stay at home In increasing numbers, couples are deciding that the dad will stay at home and the mom will go out to work. 58 Being a dad Checklist Follow these guidelines when it comes to disciplining your toddler. • Do make your demands simply and dearly. • Do say "because I say so" when you've run out of alternatives. • Do give more praise than criticism. Be specific with your praise: "Thank you for picking up your toys." • Do reserve any scolding for when you are out of earshot of others. • Don't use put-downs. • Don't compare your child with another "better" one. • Don't try to guilt-trip him about how hard life is for you. • Don't humiliate him by criticizing him in front of other children. hopeless in the kitchen, you will be able to follow a simple cake recipe better than a three-year-old and so win his admiration. If the cake is a flop, turn it into a mutual joke. And if all else fails, get a box of cake mix from the supermarket so that half the hard work is already done before you start. It doesn't matter what it is you're doing as long as the opportunity is there for closeness just to happen, for your conversation to wander into deeper realms, for questions and concerns to pop out of his mouth, for you to be able to influence him in a positive way. Let it go There are two factors to bear in mind when choosing your "dad activity" with your toddler. • Don't expect to complete what you've started. It's the doing, not the finishing, that counts. If an end result is important, wait until he (inevitably) wanders off to find mom and you can complete it on your own. DON'T MISS OUT As your baby reaches the milestones of toddlerhood, make sure you are there to share in his achievements. • Make a choice between your standards and your child. For example, if you’re gardening together, accept that you probably won't end up with a neat row of seedlings in the flower bed after your child helps you plant the seeds. If that's what you want, you should find another activity to do with your toddler. Toddlers and preschoolers 59 A MASCULINE JOB Staying at home to bring up children is becoming an increasingly acceptable and respected male role. Stay-at-home dads Although numbers remain tiny, more and more men are deciding to put being a parent ahead of their careers and opting to stay at home and care for their children. Some men have partners who earn more than they do, so it makes more sense for them to do this. Others do it because they want to. They report that it is deeply satisfying, although there may be some social isolation to overcome. Moms may be getting used to stay-at-home dads, but our ongoing preoccupation with gender makes them nervous about inviting "house- husbands" over for coffee while the children play. And male friends may tease you for being unmasculine, but it's hard to think of anything more masculine than being a good father. Single dads Single dads usually fall into two main categories: the bereaved and the divorced. Whatever the reasons, the number of households in which children live mainly with their father is increasing, and reveals a growing social and legal awareness that a single father can be just as able, loving, and effective in bringing up children as a single mother. Being a single dad isn't easy, but developing a support network of friends, relatives, community organizations, and healthcare professionals can give you practical and emotional support. Your child's pediatrician is a good place to start; he or she may be able to put you in touch with other single dads in your area. Questions & Answers As a child, my dad was the one who handed out the discipline. I don't want to fall into that role, but when my toddler is running riot, I can feel myself heading in that direction. How do I avoid this? Your own upbringing inevitably has an impact on your ideas of parenting, but don't automatically use your own father as a model for your parenting style. Discipline is important, but you must find ways that work for you and for your child. Talk to your partner and come up with a strategy that you both apply equally. Should I be disciplining my toddler, or is it too early to worry about it? No, it's not too early. Your child needs to start developing inner controls and learning how to negotiate and get along with others. Positive example is the biggest part of this, but discipline can back it up. What do I do when my toddler just will not do what I ask him to? Try to stay calm, even if others are watching. Take your child gently to a quiet spot away from the scene of the conflict. If he won t move, kneel down next to him and use a soft, reasonable voice. Explain why you are asking him to do something, and ask him to think about what he is doing and why he is doing it. With many children, this diffuses a potential conflict. I have lost my temper and shouted at my toddler. Now I feel guilty. Is this healthy? All of us crack at some stage. No parent is perfect, however they may appear. Don't be too tough on yourself. If you feel yourself boiling over, take time out. Go to another part of the room where you can keep an eye on your child and wait until your frustration has subsided. 60 Being a dad How can I avoid being a weekend dad? As the role of fathers has changed and their desire has grown to be ever more involved as equal co-parents with their partners in the upbringing of their children, society, lawmakers, and employers have struggled to keep up. Today, millions of fathers are being turned into weekend dads because of a culture of long working hours in our society. So how do you avoid becoming a weekend dad? Know your rights Family leave policies that include a father's right to take time off from work in order to spend time with a newborn and support his partner vary from place to place. Some policies are more generous than others. Find out what the law is in your area and then speak with your employer about taking time off. Stand your ground Rights are one thing, demanding them another. Male colleagues may tease you or resent the time off you get when they are still working hard at their desks or workstations. Managers may question your commitment to your career. If you really want to be there for your children, you need to be a committed advocate. Explain that you can have two loyalties— to work and to family—and that it is all about balance. Be prepared for adverse comments. WORKING AT HOME If you work at home at least some of the time, you will inevitably be around your children much more than if you work in an office five days a week. Avoid guilt At times, you may feel you're being torn in two— between home and work, your partner and your career, being a dad and making financial provisions for your family. Some feelings of guilt may enter into the equation. Try to resist it at all costs so that it does not diminish either side of your life. Push for the best work/life balance you can achieve, but don't beat yourself up if it's not perfect. GETTING INVOLVED Taking a career break to stay home and care for your child will give you a chance to be more involved in her life. Consider the alternatives If your employers really are making it tough for you to be the kind of dad you want to be, consider the alternatives (see page 57). A growing number of men take a career break and stay at home while their partners go out to work. They report that it is deeply satisfying. Other alternatives include stepping off the promotional ladder, working part-time, or working freelance so you can choose your own hours. 62 Being a dad Useful contacts UNITED STATES American Coalition for Fathers and Children 1718 M Street NW, #187 Washington, DC 20056 (800) 978-5237 www.acfc.org Information and services for fathers. SAFE TOGETHER Co-sleeping can be a rewarding experience for both you and your baby, but you must take several important safety precautions. “ Gabriel really digs in to his finger foods. I always keep a close eye on him in case he bites off more than he can chew! " MARIA, mother of 12-month-old Gabriel Eating safely 21 Eating safely Every parent knows that keeping your baby healthy means feeding him the right foods as part of a well-balanced diet, but it's also important that you prepare his food hygienically and sterilize his feeding equipment to make sure he doesn't get an upset stomach or, worse, food poisoning. Sterilizing It is important to sterilize all your baby's feeding equipment for the first six months to prevent any bacterial contamination. Before sterilizing, make sure that you wash everything (bottles, neck rings, nipples, and tops) separately in hot, soapy water, using a bottle brush and nipple cleaner. Rinse well, and either leave to drain, or dry with a clean dish towel or paper towel. Germs thrive on used and wet dish towels, so avoid these when drying your baby's feeding equipment. There are three ways of sterilizing: @ Boiling Bring a large pan of water to a boil and immerse all the bottle parts fully, making sure there are no air pockets in the bottle itself. Cover the pan and leave to boil for iO minutes. You can leave the bottle parts in the covered pan until you are ready to use them again. Alternatively, remove them and dry them with a clean towel. Boiling is the simplest and cheapest method of sterilizing, but repeated boiling can make nipples sticky, and bottles tend to get cloudy. When this happens, they should be replaced. ® Steam sterilizers With an electric steamer, you simply add the recommended amount of water and switch on. A microwave steam sterilizer works in much the same way—a cupful of water is added to the base of the sterilizer, which is then placed in the microwave for about 10 minutes. @ Dishwashers A dishwasher may be used to wash your baby's bottles and nipples, especially if it has a hot- water cycle. Omega-3 fatty acids, most notably DHA, are the best addition you can make to your diet when you’re eating for two. That’s because DHA is essential for proper brain growth and eye development in fetuses and young babies. In fact, researchers have found that toddlers whose moms consumed plenty of DHA during pregnancy had better hand-eye coordination than their peers, though it’s unclear if this translates to boosted brainpower later in childhood. Getting enough of this vital baby brain fuel in your diet is espe- cially important during the last trimester (when your baby’s brain grows at a phe- nomenal pace) and while you’re nurs - ing (the DHA content of a baby’s brain triples during the first 3 months of life). And what’s good for the expected is also good for the expecting. For you, get- ting enough DHA may mean moderated mood swings and a lowered risk of post- partum depression. Another potential postpartum perk? Getting enough DHA when you’re expecting could mean your baby will have better sleep habits later on. Luckily, DHA is found in plenty of foods you probably already eat—and like to eat: Salmon (choose wild when you can) and other higher-fat fish, such as sardines Canned light tuna Walnuts Arugula DHA-rich eggs (often called omega-3 eggs)NINE MONTHS OF EATING WELL 99 Grass-fed beef and buffalo Crab and shrimp Chicken (free-range—or pasture- raised—chickens usually have more DHA) You can also ask your practitioner about pregnancy-safe mercury-free DHA supplements (many prenatal sup- plements contain up to 200 to 300 mg of DHA already). You’re not only eating for two, but drinking for two. Your baby’s body, like yours, is composed mostly of fluids. As that little body grows, so does its demand for fluids. Your body needs fluids more than ever, too, since pregnancy pumps up fluid volume significantly. Water also eases constipation, rids your body of toxins and waste products (and baby’s, too), and reduces excessive swelling and the risk of UTIs and preterm labor. So it’s important you get enough fluids when you’re expecting.

If you’re like many expectant moms, you’ll discover that your feet are growing, too. Good news if you’re look- ing to revamp your entire shoe collec - tion—not so good if you’ve already sized out of your favorites and shopping for baby has left you cash crunched. What causes your feet to go through a growth spurt? While some expansion can be attributed to the normal fluid retention and swelling of pregnancy (or to new fat in your feet if your weight gain has been substantial or quick), there’s another reason, too. The imagined can actually be more frightening for a young child than the reality—and what he or she doesn’t know can hurt more than it has to. " LAUREN, mother of six-week-old Minnie The first few weeks 23 The first few weeks The first few weeks of your baby's life are all about adjustment—both for you and lor your baby. It's too soon to expect structured sleep patterns, or to try to impose a routine on him, so it makes sense to go with the flow and take your cues from your baby at this tender age, and enjoy every minute of these precious newborn days. His first sleep You've waited nine months to meet your baby, and now that he's here, all he seems to do is sleep. But he's just doing what comes naturally. Wakefulness for the first few hours after birth, followed by a long stretch, often up to 24 hours, of very sound sleep, is the normal newborn pattern. The majority of your baby's time at this stage will be spent sleeping and feeding, but there won't be a regular pattern to this yet. He will probably be alert only for short periods every day; he's not mature enough to benefit from longer periods of alertness, and sleep (particularly REM sleep) helps him to mature. Gradually, these periods of wakefulness will grow longer, so that by the end of the first month he may be awake for a total of two or three hours during the day, most of it in one long stretch. He may also begin to sleep for longer periods, so that instead of one or two hours, he may be able to sleep for three or four, but this is by no means the rule. Sleeping and feeding Your baby uses quite a bit of energy feeding and, as milk has a sleep- inducing effect, it's very likely that he will drift back into a contented sleep as soon as he's had his fill. Breast milk doesn’t carry germs, but it is packed with powerful antibod- ies that help your little one defend her brand new immune system from bugs of all varieties. The rest of you, however, is a dif - ferent story. You can pass germs along to your baby through other contact with her, a good reason to be even more hyper about hygiene when you’re sick. Wash your hands before you touch your baby or her stuff, as well as before feeds—and don’t forget to cover sneezes and coughs with a tissue (not your hand). Expanding Baby’s Repertoire O nce your baby is lapping up those first foods, you can expand the menu. But do it slowly, keeping these pointers in mind: Stay solo . . . and go slow. Most doc- tors recommend a one-at-a-time policy when introducing new foods. So unless your baby’s doctor has suggested a dif- ferent course for bringing on different courses, serve up new foods alone—or in combo with other foods that have already tested well. Offer a new menu item for 3 to 5 days before you bring on another—that way, if your little one shows signs of an allergy or sensitiv - ity (excessive gassiness, diarrhea or mucus in the stool, vomiting, a rough rash on the face, particularly around the mouth, a runny nose and/or watery eyes or wheezing that doesn’t seem to be associated with a cold, unusual night wakefulness or daytime crankiness), you’ll be able to figure out which food triggered it. No adverse reaction? Then you can keep the item on the menu and move on to the next new food. If you think your baby may be sen- sitive to something you’ve served, wait about a week before trying the food again (though if the reaction was severe, check with the doctor before ever serv- ing that food again). If you get a similar reaction two or three times in a row, you can probably conclude there’s a sensitivity. Eliminate that food from baby’s diet for several months, then try it again when your pediatrician gives the green light. If your baby seems to react to almost every new food you offer, or there’s a history of allergies in your fam- ily, check in with your doctor. Keep food choices simple . . . and separate. It’ll probably make sense to take action to see that the gain gets back on a sensible track, but not to stop it in its tracks. Dieting to lose weight is never appropriate when you’re pregnant, and neither is using appetite-suppressing drinks or pills (these can actually be very dangerous). I t’s not so much a law of physics as it is a law of busy motherhood: You can’t always count on your baby and your breasts being at the same place at the same time. There is a way, however, to feed your baby breast milk (and keep your milk supply up) even if you and baby are miles apart: by pumping (or expressing) milk. Wondering when you’d need or want to pump? Here are some common reasons: ■ Relieve engorgement when your milk comes in ■ Collect milk for feedings while you’re working ■ Provide relief bottles for when you’re away from home 172 THE FIRST MONTH Baby Basics at a Glance: First Month Sleeping. A newborn baby doesn’t have much of a pattern to his or her sleep schedule. Baby will be sleeping anywhere from 14 to 18 out of every 24 hours. Eating. Baby’s getting only breast milk or formula at this age: ■ Breast milk. Baby will nurse 8 to 12 times during every 24-hour period, taking in a total of anywhere from 12 to 32 ounces of breast milk (if you were counting). That’s a feeding roughly every 2 to 3 hours, timed from start of one to start of next. Feed on demand, rather than by the clock. ■ Formula. Start wit h 1 ounce at a time, 8 to 12 times per 24 hours, in the first week or so (for a total of 12 ounces). By the end of the first month, baby will probably take 2 to 3 ounces of formula per 24 hours, or 16 to 32 ounces total. Since formula takes longer to digest than breast milk, you may be able to spread out meals to one every 3 to 4 hours. Even formula-fed newborns are best fed on demand and to appetite, rather than on a schedule. Playing. A newborn baby doesn’t really need any toys (your cuddles and caresses are the best toys for your little one), but since baby can see objects 8 to 12 inches away (the distance to your face as you hold that bundle), a mobile or play gym is a good option for stimulating baby when your arms aren’t free. Babies love looking at bold patterns and faces, so if you’re able to find a mobile that combines both, even better. Your toddler still has plenty of progress to make in the coordination and dexterity depart¬ ment before he or she can be put on hygiene detail—but baby steps toward self-care are already being taken. So now that you know what a corpus luteum cyst is, you’re probably wonder- ing—how will it affect my pregnancy? The answer: It probably won’t at all. The cyst is usually nothing to worry about—or do anything about. Chances are, it will go away by itself in the sec - ond trimester. But just to be sure, your practitioner will keep an eye on its size and condition regularly via ultrasound (which means you get extra peeks at your baby). Some moms-to-be report an ovulation-like pinching sensation on one side of their lower abdomen early in pregnancy that may be related to the corpus luteum or to a corpus luteum cyst. Again, nothing to worry about, but mention it to your practitioner for reassurance.172 THE SECOND MONTH they’ve never gone before, both to exhilarating highs and depressing lows. Moods that can have you over-the-moon one moment, down-in-the-dumps the next—and weeping inexplicably over insurance commercials in between. Can you blame it on your hormones? You bet. These swings may be more pronounced in the first trimester (when hormonal havoc is at its peak) and, in general, in women who ordinarily expe- rience emotional ups and downs before their periods (it’s sort of like PMS pumped up). Feelings of ambivalence about the pregnancy once it’s confirmed are common even when a pregnancy is FOR FATHERS Rolling with Her Mood Swings W elcome to the wonderful—and sometimes wacky—world of pregnancy hormones. Wonderful because they’re working hard to nur - ture the tiny life that’s taken up resi - dence inside your partner’s belly (and that you’ll soon be cuddling in your arms). Wacky because, in addition to taking control of her body (and often making her miserable), they’re also tak- ing control of her mind—making her weepy, over-the-top excited, dispropor- tionately pissed, deliriously happy, and stressed out . . . and that’s all before lunch. Not surprisingly, an expectant mom’s mood swings are usually the most pronounced during the first trimester when those pregnancy hor - mones are in their greatest state of flux (and when she’s just getting used to them). But even once the hormones have settled down in the second and third trimesters, you can still expect to be riding the emotional roller coaster with your partner, which will continue to take her to emotional highs and lows (and fuel those occasional outbursts) right up until delivery, and beyond. So what’s an expectant dad to do? Here are some suggestions: Be patient. Pregnancy won’t last for - ever (though there will be times in the 9th month where you both may won - der if it will). This, too, shall pass, and it’ll pass a lot more pleasantly if you’re patient. In the meantime, try to keep your perspective—and do whatever you can to channel your inner saint. Don’t take her outbursts person - ally. And don’t hold them against her. They are, after all, completely out of her control. Remember, it’s the hormones talking—and crying for no apparent reason. Avoid pointing out her moods, too. Though she’s powerless to control them, she’s also probably all too aware of them. And chances are, she’s no hap- pier about them than you are. If you’re wor- ried about crying escalating to the point of breath holding, your first impulse when baby starts howling is (understandably) to panic. But the calmer you stay, the faster your little one is likely to regain his calm. Even if the breath holding has begun, being the calm in your baby’s storm can help it pass more quickly—and return less often. After all, as your little one begins to use breath holding as a parent- button pusher (and he will), not play- ing into his mini-manipulations will pay off. (What’s the point of making a scene if nobody seems to notice?) ■ Don’ t cave after a spell. On the sub - ject of mommy-and-daddy manipula- tion, if your baby knows he can get what he wants by holding his breath, he will repeat, repeat, repeat. Some research suggests that breath- holding spells can be a sign of iron defi- ciency, so check with the doctor to see if your little one’s iron supplies could be low, especially if breath holding doesn’t seem to be triggered by a tantrum or other fit of frustration. In fact, giving an iron supplement can sometimes help ease breath holding even when no defi- ciency is detected. While passing out during a breath- holding episode triggered by crying isn’t considered worrisome, check with the doctor if you need more reassurance (who wouldn’t?). Certainly, any loss of consciousness that’s not related to a cry- ing spell definitely should be evaluated. Fears “My baby used to love to watch me turn on the vacuum cleaner, but now he’s sud- denly terrified of it—and anything else that makes a loud noise.” T hat’s because he’s wising up. When your baby was younger, loud noises didn’t frighten him—even if they sometimes startled him—because he wasn’t sophisticated enough to connect loud with potentially dangerous, and potentially dangerous with scary. As his understanding of the world grows— and with it his ability to sort out (in his still evolving baby brain) what’s a legitimate threat and what isn’t—his fears grow, too. In other words, while being afraid of a vacuum cleaner may seem the definition of irrational to you, it actually represents a thinking baby’s thought process. Temperament may also play a role in fearful reactions—a THE TENTH MONTH 459 little one who’s “high sensitivity” may be especially bothered by loud noises, especially sudden ones. There are any number of things in a baby’s everyday life that, though harmlessly humdrum to you, can trig - ger terror in him: sounds (such as the roar of a vacuum cleaner, the whir of a blender, the barking of a dog, the whine of a siren, the ring of the doorbell, the flushing of a toilet, the gurgle of water draining from the bathtub), having a shirt pulled over his head, being lifted high in the air (especially if he’s begun to climb, pull up, or otherwise develop depth perception), being plunked down in a bath, the motion of a wind-up or mechanical toy, and much more. Probably all babies experience fears at some point, though some overcome them so quickly, their parents are never aware of them. Little ones who live in an especially busy, noisy environment that’s always buzzing with activity (say, one where there are older siblings and multiple pets) may be less fear prone— or they may be more likely to experience fears earlier, as well as get rid of them earlier. Temperament also plays a role, of course, as it does in most behaviors. Sooner or later, your little one will leave his baby fears behind (though an early fear of the vacuum cleaner may be sucked up by a somewhat more sophis- ticated fear—say, of monsters). Until then, you can help your baby cope with everyday fears in these ways: Don’t force facing fears.
